When divided by <imath>60</imath>, <imath>2025</imath> yields <imath>33</imath>, with a remainder of <imath>45</imath>. Since <imath>33 \equiv 9 \pmod{24}</imath>, the clock is now at <imath>9:45</imath>. 

At this time, the hour is <imath>75\%</imath> over, so the hour hand is also <imath>75\%</imath> of the way between <imath>9</imath> and <imath>10</imath>. There are <imath>360/12 = 30 ^\circ</imath> degrees between <imath>9</imath> and <imath>10</imath>, and since the hour hand is <imath>75\%</imath> of the way, it is <imath>30^\circ \cdot \frac{3}{4} = \frac{45}{2}^\circ</imath> from the minute hand, which is pointing directly at <imath>9</imath>.

We now just need to find <imath>\tan{(45/2)}</imath>. Let this be <imath>x</imath>. Using the tangent addition formula, we get that 
<cmath>\tan{45} = \frac{x + x}{1 - x\cdot x}</cmath>
<cmath>1 = \frac{2x}{1-x^2}</cmath>
<cmath>x^2+2x-1 = 0.</cmath>
Using the Quadratic Formula, and knowing <imath>x</imath> must be positive since <imath>0 < x < 90</imath>, we get <imath>x = \tan{(45/2)}= \boxed{\sqrt{2}-1}</imath>

Note: Another interesting way to find the angle between the hands at 9:45 is to use the formula <imath>30h - \frac{11}{2}m</imath>, where <imath>h</imath> is the hour and <imath>m</imath> is the minute. In this case, we get the angle is <imath>30 \cdot 9 - \frac{11}{2}(45) = \frac{540-495}{2} = \frac{45}{2}</imath> as desired.

The closest multiple of <imath>60</imath> to <imath>2025</imath> is <imath>60 \cdot 33 = 1980</imath>. <imath>33</imath>, when divided by <imath>12</imath>, leaves remainder <imath>9</imath>, thus clock depicts hour <imath>9</imath>. <imath>2025 - 1980 = 45</imath> minutes, so time is <imath>9:45</imath>. An hour has <imath>60</imath> minutes where <imath>\frac{45}{60} = 0.75</imath>, or <imath>0.75</imath> past the <imath>9</imath>th hour.

Since double <imath>22.5^{\circ}</imath> is <imath>45^{\circ}</imath>, we can use sine and cosine double angle (or addition) identities:

<cmath>\sin(2 \theta)=\sin(\theta)\cdot\cos(\theta)+\sin(\theta)\cdot\cos(\theta)=2 \sin(\theta)\cos(\theta)</cmath>
and
<cmath>\cos(2 \theta)=\cos(\theta)\cdot\cos(\theta)-\sin(\theta)\cdot\sin(\theta)=\cos^2(\theta)-\sin^2(\theta)</cmath>

Notice by dividing <imath>\cos(2 \theta)</imath> by <imath>\sin(2 \theta)</imath>, the denominator and numerator cancel a trig function, so we get...

<cmath>\frac{\cos(2 \theta)}{\sin(2 \theta)} = \frac{\cos^2(\theta)-\sin^2(\theta)}{2 \sin(\theta)\cos(\theta)}</cmath>
<cmath>\frac{2}{\tan(2 \theta)} = \frac{\cos(\theta)}{\sin(\theta)} - \frac{\sin(\theta)}{\cos(\theta)}</cmath>

Recall <imath>\theta = 22.5^{\circ}</imath> and <imath>\tan(45^{\circ}) = 1</imath>...

<cmath>2 = \frac{1}{\tan(22.5^{\circ})} - \tan(22.5^{\circ})</cmath>

Let <imath>x = \tan(22.5^{\circ})</imath>...
<cmath>2x = 1 - x^2</cmath>
<cmath>x^2 + 2x - 1 = 0</cmath>
With the quadratic formula we get:
<cmath>x = \frac{-2\pm\sqrt{4+4}}{2}=\pm\sqrt{2} - 1</cmath>
For <imath>x>0</imath> since <imath>0^{\circ}<22.5^{\circ}<90</imath>, thus we obtain <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B) } \sqrt{2}-1}</imath>

We know that the angle between the hour and minute hand follows the relationship <imath>22.5^{\circ}<30^{\circ}</imath> and thus <imath>\tan(22.5^{\circ}) < \tan(30^{\circ})</imath>, where <imath>\tan(30^{\circ}) = \frac{\sin(30^{\circ})}{\cos(30^{\circ})} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}</imath>.

Thus we can find an answer choice that is less than <imath>\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}</imath>. We know that <imath>\textbf{(A)}</imath> is wrong since <imath>\tan(22.5^{\circ})\ne 0</imath>. The other options involve <imath>\sqrt{2}</imath> which we can approximate with Babylonian Method:
<cmath>x_{n+1} = \frac{x_n + \frac{S}{x_n}}{2}</cmath>
for <imath>x_{n}</imath> is the guess for <imath>\sqrt{S}</imath> and <imath>x_{n+1}</imath> would be the next approximated guess. We will find the arrangement that contains the least possible occurrences of a color \( a \) and the most occurrences of a color \( b \), in which we will then use the circular gap theorem \( C_n A \) on all integers \( x \) such that \( x \in [a,b] \) and \( (a,b,x) \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \).

The average number of colors \( M \) is simply \( 9/3 = 3 \) (9 slots divided by 3 colors). So we see that the interval contains \( a < 3 < b \). We also have that the minimal number of colors is clearly 1 (it doesn't take much to show a case that contains only one color). The challenge is to find the maximal number, which is \( b \).

We see that there must be at least one of each color, so \( b \) can be a maximum of 6. However, we can see that 6 clearly cannot be \( b \), as if we have a configuration of 6 colors, that would mean that through the constraints in the problem, the other three colors are already uniquely determined. However, now there is no slots in the grid, and we cannot satisfy all the requirements, so \( b \le 5 \).

However, we also find that \( b \ne 5 \), as the four colors, say blue already determine 2 other colors, say yellow, which determine another 2 colors, say red. However, now there is one color left! This color must be blue (as there are 5), but if there is one blue an no yellow to satisfy the condition, then the case is simply impossible. Therefore, \( b \le 4 \).

We can try to do the same thing for 4, but we will see that \( b=4 \) satisfies the prerequisites.

Therefore, \( a=1 \) and \( b=4 \), in which we then use the circular gap theorem

<cmath>
C_n A = \frac{n}{k} \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
</cmath>

For \( n=x : x \in [a,b] \), \( (a,b,x) \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \) and \( 0 < k \le \left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor : k \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \)

And so, we do so!

For \( n=1 \), \( C_n A = 1 \) (note that every <imath>\binom{n}{0}=1</imath>)

For \( n=2 \), \( C_n A = 2 \)

For \( n=3 \), \( C_n A = 3 \)

For \( n=4 \), \( C_n A = 6 \)

Our answer is just the sum of all four of these, which is \( 6+3+2+1 \) or <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) } 12}</imath>


btw the actual theorem name for \( C_n A \) isn't actually the Circular Gap Theorem. I just call it that because I honestly don't know the name of it. It is a pretty neat theorem however, and I first learned it from this AIME problem here: [https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php?title=1983_AIME_Problems/Problem_7 1983 AIME Q7 Sol. 9].

It is apparently a closed form for the number of ways to write <imath>n</imath> as the sum of <imath>k</imath> positive circular cycles for <imath>n \ge 2</imath>, and for <imath>0<n \le 1</imath>, the value is just 1.

problem: Awnik repeatedly plays a game that has a probability of winning of
solutions:
Let the probability of a win be <imath>p</imath> and the probability of a loss be <imath>q</imath>. If the first game is a win, then we must find the expected number of further games to get a loss, which will be <imath>\frac{1}{q}</imath>. In addition to the first game played, there will be <imath>1+\frac{1}{q}</imath> games played. Therefore, the expected number of games needed to get a win on game <imath>1</imath> and then a loss is <imath>(p)\left(1+\frac{1}{q}\right).</imath>

Similarly, if the first game is a loss, we need to the find the expected number of further games to get a win, which will be <imath>\frac{1}{p}</imath>. There will be a total of <imath>1+\frac{1}{p}</imath> games played. Therefore, the expected number of games needed to get a loss on game <imath>1</imath> and then a win is <imath>(q)\left(1+\frac{1}{p}\right).</imath>

The answer is
<cmath>(p)\left(1+\frac{1}{q}\right) + (q)\left(1+\frac{1}{p}\right)</cmath>
<cmath>\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \left(1+\frac{3}{2}\right) + \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)(1+3) = \frac{5}{6} + \frac{8}{3} = \boxed{\frac{7}{2}}.</cmath>

Note that if we stop after getting at least one win and one loss, then the stopping condition is the first state change. If we start with a win, then we count the expected number of rounds until we lose and vice versa.

We use first-step analysis:
<cmath>\mathbb{E}[T]=1+\sum_{s\in \Omega}\mathbb{P}(s)\mathbb{E}[T-1|s]</cmath>
Here, we have <imath>\mathbb{P}(W)=\frac{1}{3}, \mathbb{P}(L)=\frac{2}{3}</imath>.

Using first-step analysis on each condition expectation, by the Markov property
<cmath>\mathbb{E}[T|W]=1+\mathbb{P}(W)\mathbb{E}[T|W]+\mathbb{P}(L)(0)=1+\mathbb{P}(W)\mathbb{E}[T|W]</cmath>
Solving, <imath>\mathbb{E}[T|W]=\frac{1}{1-\mathbb{P}(W)}=\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}(L)}</imath>. Similarly, <imath>\mathbb{E}[T|L]=\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}(W)}</imath>. Write <imath>p=\mathbb{P}(W)</imath>. <imath>q=\mathbb{P}(L)=1-p</imath>.
<cmath>\mathbb{E}[T]=1+\mathbb{P}(W)\mathbb{E}[T|W]+\mathbb{P}(L)\mathbb{E}[T|L]=1+p\left( \frac{1}{q} \right)+q\left( \frac{1}{p} \right)=1+\frac{p}{q}+\frac{q}{p}=1+\frac{p^2+q^2}{pq}</cmath>
We can simplify using <imath>(p+q)^2=1=p^2+q^2+2pq</imath>, giving <imath>p^2+q^2=1-2pq</imath>. Therefore,
<cmath>\mathbb{E}[T]=1+\frac{1-2pq}{pq}=1+\frac{1}{pq}-2=\frac{1}{pq}-1</cmath>
Substituting <imath>p=\frac{1}{3}</imath>, <imath>q=\frac{2}{3}</imath> yields <imath>3\cdot \frac{3}{2}-1=\boxed{\textbf{(D) } \frac{7}{2}}</imath>.

problem:
A frog hops along the number line according to the following rules:
* It starts at
solutions:
We will solve this using states. Let <imath>P_n</imath> be the probability of reaching <imath>4</imath>, given that you start from <imath>n</imath>. We want to find <imath>P_0</imath>. Of course, <imath>P_4 = 1</imath>. We also know that
<cmath>P_3  = \frac{1}{4}P_4 + \frac{1}{4}P_2</cmath>
<cmath>P_2 = \frac{1}{4}P_3 + \frac{1}{4}P_1</cmath>
<cmath>P_1 = \frac{1}{4}P_2 + \frac{1}{4}P_0</cmath>
<cmath>P_0 = \frac{1}{2}P_1.</cmath>
Solving the system, we find that <imath>P_1 = \frac{2}{97}</imath> and <imath>P_0 = \boxed{\frac{1}{97}}.</imath>

Let <imath>p(n)</imath> be the probability of reaching the end once we have reached lilypad <imath>n</imath>. These probabilities satisfy a finite difference equation

<cmath>p(n+1) - 4p(n) + p(n-1) = 0</cmath>

with boundary conditions

<cmath>\begin{align*}
2p_0 &= p_1&\text{(fixed derivative/Neumann)}\\
p_4 &= 1&\text{(fixed constant/Dirichlet).}
\end{align*}</cmath>

The difference equation's characteristic polynomial

<cmath>\lambda^2 - 4r + 1</cmath>

has roots

<cmath>2\pm \sqrt 3</cmath>

so the probabilities equal

<cmath>p(n) = A\left(2+\sqrt 3\right)^2 + B\left(2-\sqrt 3\right)^2</cmath>

for some coefficients <imath>A</imath> and <imath>B</imath>. Plugging this into the boundary conditions gives

<cmath>\begin{align*}
2(A + B) = A\left(2 + \sqrt3\right) + B\left(2 - \sqrt3\right)&\iff A=B\\
A\left(97+56\sqrt3\right) + B\left(97 - 56\sqrt3\right)=1&\iff 97(A+B) + \cancel{56(A-B)\sqrt3} = 1.
\end{align*}</cmath>

Thus,

<cmath>p(0) = A+B = \boxed{\textbf{(E)}\quad\frac{1}{97}}.</cmath>

Let <imath>P_n</imath> be the probability that the frog eventually reaches position <imath>n</imath>, given that it is at position <imath>n-1</imath>.

From position 1, the frog moves to 2 with probability <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath>, or disappears with probability <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath>. Hence
<imath>P_1 = \frac{1}{2}</imath>.

From position 2, the frog moves to 3 with probability <imath>\frac{1}{4}</imath>, back to 1 with probability <imath>\frac{1}{4}</imath>, or disappears with probability <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath>. Using <imath>P_1 = \frac{1}{2}</imath>, we have
<imath>P_2 = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{2} P_2 = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{8} P_2 \implies \frac{7}{8} P_2 = \frac{1}{4} \implies P_2 = \frac{2}{7}</imath>.

From position 3, similarly,
<imath>P_3 = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{2}{7} P_3 = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{14} P_3 \implies \frac{13}{14} P_3 = \frac{1}{4} \implies P_3 = \frac{7}{26}</imath>.

From position 4,
<imath>P_4 = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{7}{26} P_4 \implies \frac{97}{104} P_4 = \frac{1}{4} \implies P_4 = \frac{26}{97}</imath>.

Finally, multiplying the probabilities along the path from 1 to 4 (including the initial step from 0 to 1): <imath>\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{7} \cdot \frac{7}{26} \cdot \frac{26}{97} = \boxed{ \textbf{(E) } \frac1{97} }</imath>

problem: Two non-congruent triangles have the same area. Each triangle has sides of length
solutions:
<asy>
size(250);

pair A = (0,0);
pair C1 = (-9,0);
pair C2 = (9,0);
pair B = (-4.0/3.0, 4*sqrt(35)/3);

pen pen1 = blue+1.2;
pen pen2 = red+1.2;

draw(B--A--C1--cycle, pen1);
draw(B--A--C2--cycle, pen2);

dot("$A$", A, S);
dot("$C_1$", C1, SW);
dot("$C_2$", C2, SE);
dot("$B$", B, N);

label("$8$", (A+B)/2, W);
label("$9$", (A+C1)/2, S);
label("$9$", (A+C2)/2, S);
</asy>


Let the angles between the <imath>8</imath> and <imath>9</imath> sides be <imath>\theta_1</imath> and <imath>\theta_2</imath>. Relating the two triangles' areas, we get
<cmath>\frac{1}{2} \cdot 8 \cdot 9 \cdot \sin{\theta_1} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 8 \cdot 9 \cdot \sin{\theta_2}</cmath>
<cmath>\sin{\theta_1} = \sin{\theta_2}</cmath>
For this to be true, <imath>\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 180.</imath> 
We will now apply Law of Cosines to get an expression for <imath>s_1</imath> and <imath>s_2</imath> in terms of <imath>\theta_1</imath> and <imath>\theta_2</imath>. 
<cmath>s_1^2 = 8^2 + 9^2 - (2)(8)(9)\cos(\theta_1)</cmath>
<cmath>s_2^2 = 8^2 + 9^2 - (2)(8)(9)\cos(180-\theta_1).</cmath>
Noting that <imath>\cos{\theta_1} = -\cos{(180 - \theta_1)}</imath>, we can add the two equations to get that
<cmath>s_1^2 + s_2^2 = 290.</cmath>
We now need two perfect squares that add to <imath>290</imath>. After some analysis, we find <imath>121 + 169 = 290</imath>. Therefore, <imath>s_1 = 11</imath> and <imath>s_2 = 13</imath>, so our answer is <imath>11 + 13 = \boxed{24}.</imath>
Note that the <imath>\cos{\theta_1} = 1/6.</imath>  Also, note that <imath>289 + 1 = 290</imath>, but <imath>17</imath> and <imath>1</imath> are not valid side lengths due to the Triangle Inequality.

Let the third sides be <imath>a</imath> and <imath>b</imath>. Say the third sides is <imath>x</imath>, where <imath>x</imath> is a dummy variable. Then, by Heron’s Formula, the area of the triangle is
<cmath>\sqrt{\frac{x+17}{2}\cdot\frac{x+1}{2}\cdot\frac{x-1}{2}\cdot\frac{17-x}{2}}=\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{(17^2-x^2)(x^2-1^2)}</cmath>
Since the areas are the same, this value when <imath>x=a</imath> is the same as this value when <imath>x=b</imath>. In other words,
<cmath>\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{(17^2-a^2)(a^2-1^2)}=\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{(17^2-b^2)(b^2-1^2)}</cmath>
equivalent to
<cmath>(289-a^2)(a^2-1)=(289-b^2)(b^2-1)=c</cmath>
for some constant <imath>c</imath>.

But if we consider the quadratic
<cmath>(289-y)(y-1)=c</cmath>
we know that the two roots must be <imath>y=a^2</imath> and <imath>y=b^2</imath>. Expanding the quadratic, we get
<cmath>y^2-290y+289+c=0</cmath>
By Vieta’s Formulas, we must have <imath>a^2+b^2=290</imath>. Casework yields <imath>a=11,b=13</imath> (or vice versa) as the only solutions, so the sum is <imath>a+b=\boxed{\textbf{(C) } 24}</imath>.

Denote the angle that is between side lengths <imath>8</imath> and <imath>9</imath> as angle <imath>A</imath>, the other triangle will be <imath>180^\circ - A</imath>, because by the area formula of <imath>\frac{1}{2}a\cdot b\cdot\sin C</imath>, the <imath>\sin C</imath> needs to remain constant while <imath>a</imath> and <imath>b</imath> stay the same to keep the area the same. Denote the shorter third side as <imath>x</imath> and longer third side as <imath>y</imath>.

By applying the Law of Cosines, <imath>y^2 = 8^2 + 9^2 - 2 \cdot 8 \cdot 9 \cdot \cos(180- A)</imath>, which gives <imath>y^2 = 145 + 144\cos A</imath>. Similarly, <imath>x^2 = 145 - 144\cos A</imath>. Since the question says the third lengths are both integers, try testing values of <imath>\cos A</imath>. Notice when <imath>\cos A = \frac{1}{6}</imath>, <imath>y^2 = 169</imath> and <imath>x^2 = 121</imath>, giving the lengths as <imath>13</imath> and <imath>11</imath> respectively. The required answer is then <imath>13 + 11 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) } 24}</imath>.

As in other solutions, use sine law to check <imath>\beta=180-\alpha</imath>, <imath>\cos\alpha=-\cos\beta</imath>. Apply cosine law <imath>x^2,y^2=8^2+9^2\mp 2(8)(9)\cos\alpha=145\mp 144\cos\alpha</imath> and and verify integer solutions to <imath>x^2+y^2=2(8^2+9^2)=290</imath>.

Since <imath>\alpha>0</imath>, we need <imath>\cos\alpha<1</imath> so <imath>(1,289)=(1^2,17^2)</imath> is not valid. WLOG <imath>2\le x<y\le 16</imath>. To help with the bash, note the quadratic residues mod <imath>3</imath> and <imath>4</imath> are <imath>0,1</imath>, so it must be <imath>1+1\equiv 2</imath>, so we only need to check odd cases not divisible by <imath>3</imath>, so <imath>x=5,7,11,13</imath>.

<imath>290-25=265</imath> bad

<imath>290-49=241</imath> bad

<imath>290-121=169</imath> good, stop by symmetry.

So <imath>(x,y)=(11,13)</imath>, giving <imath>x+y=11+13=\boxed{\textbf{(C) } 24}</imath>.

Consider arbitrary such triangle with third size \(x\). By Heron's formula, the area of this triangle is
<cmath>
\sqrt{\left(\frac{17+x}{2}\right)\left(\frac{17-x}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1+x}{2}\right)\left(\frac{-1+x}{2}\right)}
</cmath>
By the triangle inequality, we have \(2 \leq x \leq 16\), which means there are few enough possibilities of \(x\) that tabling becomes a viable strategy. Consider setting up a table such as:
<cmath>
    \begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
    \text{Row}&17-x&x+17&x+1&x-1 \\
    \hline 
    A_1&15& 19& 3&  1\\
    A_2&14& 20& 4&  2\\
    A_3&13& 21& 5&  3\\
    A_4&12& 22& 6&  4\\
    A_5&11& 23& 7&  5\\
    A_6&10& 24& 8&  6\\
    A_7&9&  25& 9&  7\\
    A_8&8&  26& 10& 8\\
    A_9&7&  27& 11& 9\\
    A_{10}&6&  28& 12& 10\\
    A_{11}&5&  29& 13& 11\\
    \hline
    B_{1}&4&  30& 14& 12\\
    B_{2}&3&  31& 15& 13\\
    B_{3}&2&  32& 16& 14\\
    B_{4}&1&  33& 17& 15\\
    \end{array}
</cmath>
As \(x\) goes from \(2\to 16\), we know the area will increase, peak, and then decrease. Thus, the two possible side lengths with the same area must occur on opposite sides of the side length \(s\) that maximizes the area. The area is maximized when 8 and 9 are legs of a right triangle (Why?*), giving a side length of \(\sqrt{8^2+9^2}=\sqrt{145}\). Thus, \(12 < s < 13\), and we can divide the table in two parts, split at \(x=s\). Denote the top part \(A\) and the bottom part \(B\).

The final step is to find some rows \(A_i\) and \(B_j\) of the table that match in product. This is easier than it seems at first if we proceed by eliminating rows from \(B\):

<imath>\quad\bullet</imath> \(B_2\) contains a factor of 31, which is not present in \(A\)

<imath>\quad\bullet</imath> \(B_3\) contains 11 factors of 2, which does not occur for any row in \(A\)

<imath>\quad\bullet</imath> \(B_4\) contains a factor of 17, which is not present in \(A\)

Thus, \(B_1\) is the only valid row remaining, occurring at \(x=13\). We quickly** find the matching row in \(A\) to be \(A_{10}\), occurring at \(x=11\). Thus, we arrive at an answer of \(13+11=\boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ 24}\).

(*) Think about how you would maximize an area using \(\frac 12 ab\sin(C)\).

(**) As \(B_1\) is so close to the maximum, it is likely that the corresponding row in \(A\) will be as well, so if we start at \(A_{11}\) and work our way down, we find \(A_{10}\) on our second try.

problem: What is the greatest possible area of the triangle in the complex plane with vertices
solutions:
Because we can factor <imath>z</imath> from each vertex, the area of the triangle is equal to <imath>|z|^2</imath> multiplied by the area of the triangle with vertices <imath>2, 1+i, 1-i</imath>. 

The vertical side of that triangle has length <imath>2</imath> and the altitude to that side has length <imath>1</imath>, so the area is <imath>1</imath>. We now just need the maximum possible value of <imath>|z|^2</imath>.

The equation <imath>|4z-2| = 1</imath> can be rewritten as <imath>|z-1/2| = 1/4</imath>. Therefore, it exists as a circle with radius <imath>1/4</imath> and center at <imath>(1/2, 0)</imath> on the complex plane. The maximum possible magnitude of a complex number on this circle occurs with <imath>\frac{3}{4}</imath>, with magnitude <imath>\frac{3}{4}</imath>. We can justify this because the line connecting the origin and the complex number <imath>\frac{3}{4}</imath> goes through the center of the circle.

Our answer is then <imath>\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2 = \boxed{\frac{9}{16}}.</imath>

Rewrite the second and the third complex number, we get: <imath>\sqrt{2}e^{i\frac{\pi}{4}}z</imath>, <imath>\sqrt{2}e^{-i\frac{\pi}{4}}z</imath>. This means that the other two complex numbers both form a <imath>45^{\circ}</imath> angle with complex numbers both form <imath>2z</imath>. Also notice that the magnitude of the first complex number is <imath>2|z|</imath>, and the second and third complex numbers both have magnitude <imath>\sqrt{2}|z|</imath>, this means that these three points form an isosceles right triangle. Therefore the area for this triangle is simply just <imath>\frac{1}{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}|z|\cdot\sqrt{2}|z|=|z|^{2}</imath>. 
Now since we have <imath>|4z-2|=1</imath>, we can set 
<cmath>4z-2=e^{i\theta},\theta\in[0,2\pi)</cmath>
Therefore
<cmath>z=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{e^{i\theta}}{4}</cmath>, <cmath>|z|=\frac{1}{4}|2+e^{i\theta}|=\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{5+4\cos\theta}\le\frac{3}{4}</cmath>
<imath>\Rightarrow</imath> <cmath>Area\le \boxed{\textbf{(C)} \ \frac{9}{16}}</cmath>

Notice that there are <imath>z</imath> distinct remainders modulo <imath>z</imath>. However, if we let <imath>R(x)</imath> denote the remainder when <imath>2025x</imath> is divided by <imath>z</imath>, we know that by the problem condition,
<cmath>R(0)<R(1)<R(2)<\cdots<R(z-1)</cmath>
But there are only <imath>z</imath> distinct remainders, and each of the <imath>z</imath> terms above must correspond to a distinct remainder, so we must have <imath>R(k)=k</imath> for all <imath>k=0,1,\dots,z-1</imath>. Then <imath>2025k\equiv k\pmod{z}</imath>, so <imath>2024k\equiv 0\pmod{z}</imath>. Since <imath>k</imath> can vary, this is equivalent to <imath>2024\equiv 0\pmod{z}</imath>, or <imath>z\mid 2024</imath>.

Therefore, the values <imath>z</imath> that satisfy the property are the factors of <imath>2024</imath>, so we simply need to find the sum of the factors of <imath>2024</imath> and subtract <imath>1</imath> at the end since <imath>z\ne 1</imath>. But <imath>2024=2^3\cdot 11\cdot 23</imath>, so the sum of the factors minus <imath>1</imath> is
<cmath>(1+2+4+8)(1+11)(1+23)-1=15\cdot12\cdot24-1=4320-1=\boxed{\textbf{(E)}

Notice that <imath>2025x \equiv x \pmod{z} \, \forall z \mid 2024</imath>. Since <imath>x<y<z</imath>, all pairs <imath>(x,y)</imath> satisfy the remainder condition when <imath>z\mid 2024</imath> except for <imath>z=1</imath>. Recall that <imath>2024=2^3\cdot 11 \cdot 23</imath>, so <imath>\sum z=(15)(12)(24)-1=\boxed{\textbf{(E)}

We will show that the <imath>z</imath>'s sastifying the statement are actually all <imath>z>1</imath> and <imath>2025=1</imath> <imath>(</imath>mod <imath>z)</imath>.


We first provide the construction. Let the remainder of <imath>2025</imath> divided by <imath>z</imath> be <imath>p</imath>. We have <imath>p<z</imath>. Assume that <imath>p\geq{1}</imath> in the following steps.


<imath>2025x=px</imath> <imath>(</imath>mod <imath>z)</imath>.

<imath>2025y=py</imath> <imath>(</imath>mod <imath>z)</imath>.


The aim of the construction is to make the the remainder of <imath>px</imath> upon division by <imath>z</imath> as large as possible, and to make the remainder of <imath>py</imath> upon division by <imath>z</imath> as small as possible.


【The Construction】


Set <imath>x</imath> to be the largest positive integer satisfying <imath>px<z</imath>.

Set <imath>y</imath> equal to <imath>x+1</imath>. 


【Proof of why the contruction works】


<imath>py=p(x+1)\geq{z}</imath>.


Now calculate the remainder of <imath>2025y</imath> divided by <imath>z</imath>. We have <imath>p(x+1)=px+p\leq{2px}<2z</imath>, so the remainder of <imath>p(x+1)</imath> upon division by <imath>z</imath> is simply <imath>p(x+1)-z=px+p-z<px</imath>.


The remainder of <imath>2025x</imath> divided by <imath>z</imath> is <imath>px</imath>, while the remainder of <imath>2025y</imath> divided by <imath>z</imath> is less than <imath>px</imath>. This is a success in finding a counterexample, but we have to ensure that this pair of <imath>(x,y)</imath> satisfies the condition <imath>x<y<z</imath>.


Since <imath>px<z</imath>, <imath>x<\frac{z}{p}</imath>, <imath>y<\frac{z}{p}+1</imath>. If <imath>p\geq{2}</imath>, we have <imath>y<\frac{z}{2}+1</imath>, <imath>y<\frac{z}{2}+1<z</imath> for all <imath>z\geq{3}</imath>. For <imath>z=2</imath>, a simple manual check of <imath>x=0</imath> and <imath>y=1</imath> works as this is the only possible pair.



This explains why the construction fails when <imath>p=1</imath>. If <imath>p=1</imath> we have <imath>x=z-1</imath> and <imath>y=z</imath>, but the condition requires <imath>y<z</imath>.


In fact, for <imath>p=1</imath>, <imath>2025x=x</imath> <imath>(</imath>mod <imath>z)</imath>, <imath>2025y=y</imath> <imath>(</imath>mod <imath>z)</imath>. The remainders are simply <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath> themselves, the problem statement is automatically true for any pair of <imath>(x,y)</imath> with <imath>x<y</imath>.


For <imath>p=0</imath>, <imath>2025x=0</imath> <imath>(</imath>mod <imath>z)</imath>, <imath>2025y=0</imath> <imath>(</imath>mod <imath>z)</imath>. The statement is always false because both remainders are always <imath>0</imath>.



In the end, we identify and add all the possible values of <imath>z</imath> together.


<imath>2025=kz+1</imath> for some positive integer <imath>k</imath>

<imath>kz=2024</imath>

<imath>kz=2^3\times{11}\times{23}</imath>


In the end, do not forget that <imath>z=1</imath> is not included. The answer is <imath>4320-1=4319</imath>.

problem: How many real numbers satisfy the equation
solutions: Let f(x)=\sin(20\pi x) and g(x)=\log_{20}(x). Note that g passes through \left(\frac{1}{20},-1\right) and (1,0) and (20,1); these are the extrema and midpoint of f. We want to find the number of intersections of f and g. Let an occurrence of sine passing under the x-axis a down-dip, and similarly define an up-dip. We find that the period of f is \frac{1}{10}, so between x=\frac{1}{20} and x=1 the number of periods is 9.5. The first period indeed counts, so effectively we have 10 down-dips in this interval. Each down-dip contributes 2 to the total, so we have 20 total intersections. From x=1 to x=20, there are 190 periods, each of which also contributes 2 to the total due to the up-dips. Therefore, this case contributes 380 points to the total. But (1,0) is counted in both cases, so the total is 20+380-1=\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 399}.

Note that the number of solutions to <imath> \sin(20\pi x) = \log_{20}(x) </imath> is the same as asking the number of intersection points of the graphs <imath> \sin(20\pi x) </imath> and <imath> \log_{20}(x) </imath>.

We begin by understanding the range of <imath> \sin(20\pi x) </imath>. The range is just <imath> -1 \le \sin(20\pi x) \le 1 </imath>.

For the graph <imath> \log_{20}(x) </imath> to intersect <imath> \sin(20\pi x) </imath>, we need <imath> \log_{20}(x) </imath> to also be in the range <imath> -1 \le \log_{20}(x) \le 1 </imath>, which is simplified into <imath> \frac{1}{20} \le x \le 20 </imath>.

The period of <imath> \sin(20\pi x) </imath> is <imath> \frac{2\pi}{20\pi} = \frac{1}{10} </imath>. Thus in every 1 unit, there are 10 periods.

Also, the x intersections of both graphs are the same. <imath> \sin(20\pi x) = 0 </imath> indicates <imath> x = \frac{1}{2} + k </imath>. Also, <imath> \log_{20}(x) = 0 </imath> if <imath> x = 1 </imath>, so we have <imath> k = 0 </imath> and we must consider two cases, either <imath> \frac{1}{20} \le x \le 1 </imath> and <imath> 1 < x \le 20 </imath>.

Case 1: <imath> \frac{1}{20} \le x \le 1 </imath>.

For this case, we first must understand one thing. Does <imath> \log_{20}(x) </imath> intersect the first time <imath> \sin(20\pi x) </imath> dips below the x-axis for <imath> x \ge 0 </imath> 0 times, 1 time, or 2 times?

Well, notice that if we plug in <imath> x = \frac{1}{20} </imath>, <imath> \sin(20\pi x) = 0 </imath> and <imath> \log_{20}(x) = -1 </imath>, so because <imath> \log_{20}(x) </imath> is increasing, it will intersect the graph of <imath> \sin(20\pi x) </imath> twice.

Taking this into consideration, in each period, half the period is positive whereas the other half is negative. Then, because there are 10 periods between <imath> \frac{1}{20} \le x \le 1 </imath>, there will be 10 negative periods.

Then, the graph <imath> \log_{20}(x) </imath> intersects these 10 periods twice, giving us a total of 20 intersections in this case.

Case 2: <imath> 1 < x \le 20 </imath>.

For this case, we see that there is a total of 10 periods per unit, and there are <imath> 20 - 1 = 19 </imath> units. Then, because once again there are 10 positive intervals, <imath> \log_{20}(x) </imath> will intersect each interval twice, giving us a total of 20 intersections per one unit. Multiplying by 19, we get a total of <imath> 19 \times 20 = 380 </imath> intersections. However, we have excluded 1, and the first period lasting <imath> 1 \le x \le \frac{11}{10} </imath>, we see that two intersections occur, one at the point (1,0) and another at some random point. We already considered the point (1,0) last case, so we subtract 1 from the total to obtain <imath>380 - 1 = 379</imath>.

Thus the total number of solutions to the equation is <imath> 20 + 379 = </imath><imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 399}</imath>.

Each period of the sin function is <imath>\frac{1}{10}</imath>, so 200 periods, 2 intersections each (just draw it out) - 400. But there is 1 overlap in two periods at <imath>(1,0)</imath>, so subtract 1 -> 399 (can check end behavior if time)

Note that <imath>-1\le \sin 20\pi x=\log_{20} x\le 1</imath>, forcing <imath>\frac{1}{20}\le x\le 20</imath>. For simplicity, let <imath>2\pi t=20\pi x</imath> or <imath>t=10x\in\left[ \frac{1}{2},200 \right]</imath>. Since <imath>2\pi t</imath> is the unit-period parametrization, there are <imath>200</imath> full periods on <imath>[0,200]</imath>, and we check the closed intervals <imath>\left[ \frac{1}{2},1 \right],[1,2],\dots,[199,200]</imath>. By sketching the graph, we see that when sine and log share the same sign, the sine will weave through the log twice for the non-degenerate case. The endpoints are also non-degenerate after verifying <imath>\log\left( \frac{1}{20} \right)=-1,\log_{20}20=1</imath> whereas <imath>\sin 20\pi \left( \frac{1}{20} \right)=\sin 20\pi(200)=0</imath>.

Because <imath>\log_{20}(x=1)=0=\log_{20}(t=10)</imath> lands perfectly on an integer, by the intermediate value theorem, <imath>\log</imath> will only have at most two signs among <imath>-,0,+</imath> in each full period closed interval. We count <imath>200\cdot 2=400</imath> intersections. However, <imath>t=10</imath> is shared among <imath>[9,10]</imath> and <imath>[10,11]</imath> so we must subtract the overlap to get <imath>400-1=\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 399}</imath>.

We know that the period of <imath>\sin(20\pi x)</imath> is <imath>\frac{2\pi}{20\pi}=\frac{1}{10}</imath>, and that the amplitude of the graph is 1. Now, we  need to find the values of x for which the graph of <imath>y=\log_{20} x</imath> intersects with the upper and lower extrema of <imath>\sin(20\pi x)</imath>, or with <imath>y=1</imath> and <imath>y=-1</imath>. At <imath>y=-1</imath>, <imath>x=20^{-1}=\frac{1}{20}</imath>, and at <imath>y=1</imath>, <imath>x=20^1=20</imath>. We know that for each period of the sin graph, there will be 2 intersections, and there are <imath>\frac{20}{\frac{1}{10}}=200</imath> periods of the sin graph from 0 to 20. Because there are 3 answer choices close to 400, we can test with smaller bounds using a line, and count the points. The line from <imath>(\frac{1}{20},-1)</imath> to <imath>(\frac{1}{2},1)</imath> intersected the graph <imath>y=\sin(20\pi x)</imath> 9 times, and there were 5 periods between <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath> and <imath>0</imath>, thus we can say the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 399}</imath>

Let <imath>\triangle ABC</imath> and center <imath>O</imath> be such that <imath>OA=1, OB=2, OC=3</imath>. Suppose the length of the side of <imath>ABC</imath> is <imath>s</imath>. Noticing that <imath>OA + OB = OC</imath>, we suspect that <imath>OACB</imath> is a cyclic quadrilateral. If it was, we could apply Ptolemy's Theorem, which would say that 
<cmath>CB \cdot OA + OB \cdot AC = OC \cdot AB</cmath>
<cmath>s + 2s = 3s.</cmath>
Because Ptolemy's is true, <imath>OACB</imath> is cyclic. Because it's cyclic,  <imath>\angle AOB = 180 - \angle BCA = 120</imath>. Applying Law of Cosines on <imath>AOB</imath>, we get 
<cmath>s^2 = 1^2 + 2^2 - 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 2 \cdot \cos{120}</cmath>
<cmath>s^2 = 1 + 4 +2 = \boxed{7}.</cmath>

Call the point that lies on the circle <imath>r = 1</imath> as <imath>A</imath>, <imath>r = 2</imath> as <imath>B</imath> and <imath>r = 3</imath> as <imath>C</imath>. 

We could set <imath>A = (1, 0)</imath>, <imath>B = (2\cos B, 2\sin B)</imath> and <imath>C = (3\cos C, 3\sin C)</imath>

<imath>s = BA = CB = CA</imath>.

<cmath>BA = (2\cos B - 1)^2 + (2\sin B)^2 = 5 - 4\cos B</cmath>

<cmath>CA = (3\cos C - 1)^2 + (3\sin C)^2 = 10 - 6\cos C</cmath>

<cmath>CB = (3\cos C - 2\cos B)^2 + (3\sin C - 2\sin B)^2 = 13 - 12\cos(B - C)</cmath>

Let <imath>\cos B = x</imath> and <imath>\cos C = y</imath> for easier representation

Because <imath>5 - 4\cos B = 10 - 6\cos C</imath>, hence <imath>x =\frac{6y-5}{4}</imath>

Also, <imath>5 - 4\cos B = 13 - 12\cos(B - C)</imath>, which <imath>12\cos(B - C) = 8 + 4\cos B = 8 + 4\cdot\frac{6y-5}{4} = 3 + 6y</imath>, leading to <imath>\cos(B - C) = \frac{1+2y}{4}</imath>

Noting that <cmath>\cos(B - C) = xy + \sqrt{1-x^{2}}\sqrt{1-y^{2}} = \frac{1+2y}{4}</cmath>
<cmath>1 - x^2 = 1 - (\frac{6y-5}{4})^2 = \frac{-36y^2 + 60y - 9}{16}</cmath>

let <imath>K= \sqrt{1-x^{2}}\sqrt{1-y^{2}}</imath>, which the equation <imath>xy + \sqrt{1-x^{2}}\sqrt{1-y^{2}} = \frac{1+2y}{4}</imath> can be simplified to <imath>\frac{y(6y-5)}{4} + K = \frac{1+2y}{4}</imath>

By rearranging, the equation <imath>\frac{y(6y-5)}{4} + K = \frac{1+2y}{4}</imath> turns into <imath>K = \frac{-6y^2 + 7y + 1}{4}</imath>

Squaring both sides, which <cmath>K^2 = (1 - x^2)(1 - y^2) = \frac{(-6y^2 + 7y + 1)^2}{16}</cmath>
Substituting in <imath>1 - x^2 = \frac{-36y^2 + 60y - 9}{16}</imath>, we get <cmath>(-6y^2 + 7y + 1)^2 = (-36y^2 + 60y - 9)(1 - y^2)</cmath>

By expanding, <imath>LHS = 36y^4 - 84y^3 + 37y^2 + 14y + 1</imath> and <imath>RHS = 36y^4 - 60y^3 - 27y^2 + 60y - 9</imath>

Rearrange it, we get <cmath>12y^3 - 32y^2 + 23y - 5 = 0</cmath>

By inspection (which <imath>y</imath> cant be greater than 1 because it is a cosine value), let’s try <imath>y = \frac{1}{2}</imath>: it is a root. 

By polynomial division, this becomes <cmath>(2y - 1)(6y^2 - 13y + 5) = 0</cmath>

The other <imath>2</imath> solutions from the quadratic are <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath> and <imath>\frac{5}{3}</imath> (greater than <imath>1</imath>, rejected), meaning that the only <imath>y</imath> possible value is <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath>. 

Because length of <imath>CA = (3\cos C - 1)^2 + (3\sin C)^2 = 10 - 6\cos C</imath>, hence the answer is <imath>10 - 6(1/2) = 10 - 3 = \boxed{\textbf{(E)} \ 7}. </imath>

Let <imath>A</imath> be a point on the circle with radius <imath>1</imath>, <imath>B</imath> be a point on the circle with radius <imath>2</imath>, <imath>C</imath> be a point on the circle with radius <imath>3</imath>. Call the shared center for these three circles <imath>O</imath>. First let’s check if <imath>O</imath> is in <imath>\triangle ABC</imath>.
Rotate <imath>OA</imath> clockwise by <imath>60^{\circ}</imath> to <imath>OA’</imath>, then it is equivalent to check if point <imath>A’</imath> is outside <imath>\triangle ABC</imath>.
Assume that <imath>A’</imath> is outside <imath>\triangle ABC</imath>, easy to prove that <imath>\triangle AOC\cong \triangle AA’B</imath>. Therefore <imath>OC=A’B=3</imath>, in <imath>\triangle OA’B</imath>,
<cmath>OA’+OB=1+2=3=A’B</cmath>
This violates the triangle inequality. Thus <imath>A’</imath> must be inside <imath>\triangle ABC</imath> in order to let the shape make sense.
Easy to prove <imath>\triangle AOB\cong \triangle AA’C</imath>, therefore <imath>A’C=2</imath>. And by rotation <imath>OA’=1</imath>. Also notice that <imath>OC=3</imath>, which means <imath>OA’+A’C=OC</imath>, this means <imath>O</imath>, <imath>A’</imath>, <imath>C</imath> must be collinear. Since <imath>\angle AOA’=\angle AA’O=60^{\circ}</imath>, <imath>\angle AA’C=120^{\circ}</imath>, then use Law of Cosines in <imath>\triangle AA’C</imath>:
<cmath>s^{2}=AC^{2}=1^{2}+2^{2}-2\cdot 1\cdot{2}\cdot\cos 120^{\circ}=\boxed{\textbf{(E)} \ 7}</cmath>

Let <imath>O</imath> be the common center and let the vertices of the triangle <imath>A,B,C</imath> satisfy <imath>OA=1</imath>, <imath>OB=2</imath>, <imath>OC=3</imath>, with side length <imath>AB=BC=CA=s</imath>. Let <imath>x=s^{2}</imath>. Let <imath>\alpha=\angle AOB</imath>, <imath>\beta=\angle BOC</imath>, <imath>\gamma=\angle COA</imath>, so <imath>\alpha+\beta+\gamma=360^\circ</imath>. By the Law of Cosines,

<cmath>x = 1^2+2^2-2\cdot1\cdot2\cos\alpha = 5-4\cos\alpha \Rightarrow \cos\alpha = \frac{5-x}{4}</cmath>
<cmath>x = 2^2+3^2-2\cdot2\cdot3\cos\beta = 13-12\cos\beta \Rightarrow \cos\beta = \frac{13-x}{12}</cmath>
<cmath>x = 3^2+1^2-2\cdot3\cdot1\cos\gamma = 10-6\cos\gamma \Rightarrow \cos\gamma = \frac{10-x}{6}</cmath>

For angles summing to <imath>360^\circ</imath>, we have

<cmath>\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma - 2\cos\alpha\cos\beta\cos\gamma = 1</cmath>
Substitute <imath>\cos\alpha,\cos\beta,\cos\gamma</imath> in terms of <imath>x</imath> and plug in answer choices (don't bother trying to solve it), we get <imath>x = \boxed{7}</imath>.

Let <imath>\omega_1</imath> be a circle of radius <imath>1</imath> centered at <imath>O=(0, 0)</imath>. Let <imath>\omega_2</imath> be a circle of radius <imath>2</imath> centered at <imath>(0, 0)</imath>. Let <imath>A</imath> be the point <imath>(0, 3)</imath>. Let <imath>B</imath> be some point on <imath>\omega_1</imath>. Let <imath>C</imath> be some point in the plane such that <imath>ABC</imath> is equilateral. Our goal is to find some <imath>C</imath> that lies on <imath>\omega_2</imath>. 

Because <imath>\angle BAC=60^\circ</imath> and <imath>AB=AC</imath>, we see that <imath>C</imath> must be the rotation of <imath>B</imath> around <imath>A</imath>, either <imath>60^\circ</imath> clockwise or counterclockwise. Note that because the locus of all points <imath>B</imath> is <imath>\omega_1</imath>, the locus of all points <imath>C</imath> is the two circles formed by rotating <imath>\omega_1</imath> <imath>60^\circ</imath> around <imath>A</imath>, either direction. 

We want a <imath>C</imath> that lies on <imath>\omega_2</imath>, so we naturally intersect <imath>\omega_2</imath> with one of these two circles (I chose the one that's rotated counterclockwise because the numbers are nicer). We could easily calculate the intersections using coord geo, but notice that the problem asks for a unique <imath>s</imath>; this means that the circle is tangent to <imath>\omega_2</imath>. The tangent point, which is the only <imath>C</imath> that works, lies on the line connecting the centers. The center (denote it <imath>O'</imath>) of (half of) <imath>C</imath>'s locus is the center of <imath>\omega_2</imath> rotated <imath>60^\circ</imath> counterclockwise. Because <imath>AO=AO'</imath> and <imath>\angle OAO'=60^\circ</imath>, we see <imath>\triangle OAO'</imath> is equilateral, meaning <imath>\angle AOO'=\angle AOC=60^\circ</imath>, which means by extension that <imath>C</imath> is <imath>30^\circ</imath> counterclockwise from the horizontal. <imath>OC=2</imath> as <imath>C</imath> lies on <imath>\omega_2</imath>, so the coordinates of <imath>C</imath> are at <imath>(2\cos 30^\circ, 2\sin 30^\circ)=(\sqrt{3}, 1)</imath>. <imath>A</imath> is at <imath>(0, 3)</imath>, and a quick distance formula gives us <imath>s^2=(C.x-A.x)^2+(C.y+A.y)^2=3+4=\boxed{7}</imath>.
